1.pericope_label: Paul an apostle by the will of God, to Timothy his dearly beloved son

schools.summary: Settle the date before the exegesis, because the letter reads differently depending on it. Lay out both sides honestly — Lardner, Lightfoot and Hammond for the first Roman imprisonment, Paley and Macknight for a second — and give the two arguments that decide it: in the earlier letters Paul confidently expects release and asks Philemon to prepare a lodging, while here he is ready to be offered; and Onesiphorus had to seek him out very diligently, which suits close confinement rather than the hired house of Acts. On the salutation, press the preposition before the promise of life: it states the object of the appointment, to publish abroad eternal life, and it is worth pausing on a letter written under expectation of death that opens on life. Note also the changed epithet — beloved son here, own son in the first letter — and that Paul had used the same word of Timothy when writing to Corinth, an incidental corroboration of authorship.

Ask why the lofty titles are used at all in writing to one man who needed no convincing, and answer that Timothy was not the only person in view: being near death, Paul lays claim to the authority belonging to his public character, so that the whole course of his ministry may be ratified. Use the promise of life to reach backwards — it was given to the fathers in ancient times, so the faith of men under the law must have looked toward Christ, what the promises contained being suspended until it was exhibited in him. And set the reader in the right posture before the epistle: let Paul's condition come before our eyes as we read, a man looking for nothing but to die for the gospel as its standard-bearer.

Take the date question seriously and say which authorities stand where, then give the reason for preferring a second imprisonment; and answer the alternative on the ground of character rather than evidence, since to say Paul merely despaired at first and grew hopeful later makes him a man subject to alarms, which the rest of his conduct contradicts. On the salutation itself keep it brief: the commission was of God's will, not man's, and the sonship is spiritual, resting on instruction given rather than on conversion wrought.

Keep the inscription plain and doctrinal. The apostleship came merely of God's good pleasure and by a grace Paul professes himself unworthy of. The gospel is the promise of life in Christ Jesus — life the end and Christ the way — and every promise of God is in him yea and amen, so that we may depend on them safely. Note that grace and mercy and peace come from the Father and from Christ together, which is why both are to be applied to for them; and that even a Timothy needed these blessings, so they are the best things we can ask for those we love best.

Begin by asking why there is a second letter at all, and answer it from the first: Paul had written that he hoped to come shortly, the visit never happened, and so he consoles by writing instead of coming. Show the reader who is being consoled — a man grieving at the absence and weighed down by a charge just taken up — and generalise it, since even great men set at the helm feel the strangeness of the position and are overwhelmed as by waves of business. Note the marks that the end was near, that Paul says he is ready to be offered and that at his first answer no man stood with him, and that he not only writes but asks Timothy to come, and to bring the books and above all the parchments.

debates.question: Where does the promise of life stand in relation to the old covenant?

sides.position: The promise was given to the fathers in ancient times, so the faith of men under the law looked toward Christ; what the promises contained was in some respects suspended until it was exhibited in him
The gospel simply is the promise of life in Christ Jesus, life the end and Christ the way, and all the promises of God are in him yea and amen
The preposition states the object of the apostleship — Paul was appointed in order to publish abroad the promise of eternal life — and that life takes in the present as much as the future

outliers.note: Alone tells the reader what this letter has meant to him personally, saying that it has been more profitable to him than any other book of Scripture, and alone gives a rule for reading it — that Paul's condition at the time should come before our eyes, a man looking for nothing but to die for the testimony of the gospel as its standard-bearer.

Alone turns the changed epithet into an argument about authorship: Paul had already called Timothy beloved when writing to Corinth, which he treats as incidental but strong proof that Paul is the writer here, the affectionate relation the Pastorals assume being independently attested in Acts and the earlier letters.

Alone hears the appeal to the sovereign will as the keynote of the whole epistle, in harmony with the calm resignation breathing through it — the office having come apart from any merit of Paul's own, who neither aspired to it nor wished for it — and alone reads the softened address as a sign that Paul knew these lines were in reality his farewell.

Alone asks what occasioned a second letter and answers it from the promise of a visit in the first that was never kept, and alone describes the state of the recipient: a man newly at the helm, feeling the strangeness of the position and overwhelmed as by waves of business, at a time when the ground was everywhere unturned.

themes: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus,
To Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

3.pericope_label: Night and day remembrance: the unfeigned faith of Lois and Eunice

schools.summary: Untangle the sentence before preaching it: a long parenthesis separates the thanksgiving from its object, and what Paul thanks God for is the unfeigned faith of Timothy named two verses later. Note in passing that the idiom for giving thanks here is not the one Paul normally uses. Take the forefathers as the members of his own family whose devotion he inherited, not as the patriarchs of the race. On the tears, settle for the last parting and cite the leave-taking at Miletus as evidence that Paul left strong men weeping. Then make the argument the two named women actually support: Luke names neither Lois nor Eunice and reports only that the mother believed and the father was a Greek, while Paul names both and passes the father over — neither account built from the other, which is an undesigned coincidence and evidence for the genuineness of each. Add that the word for being reminded means a reminder received from another, so somebody had brought Paul news.

Keep the thanksgiving where it belongs, as praise to God for a gift that is his and not Timothy's own, since every good thing comes from him and none may glory as though he had not received it. Then take the faith itself as the grace implanted by the Spirit in the heart, genuine and sincere, believing unto righteousness and working by love to God and to his people, and attended by good works — which is what distinguishes it from the feigned kind the epistle everywhere warns against.

On the pure conscience make the point that costs something: Paul had always aimed to please God according to the light he had, even in the time when through ignorance he persecuted the church. Take the ancestry as a comfort rather than an argument — one who stands on the verge of life is much refreshed by the remembrance of the predecessors he is going to. Then use the family to teach: the names are both Grecian and indeed heathen, so the mother, Jewess though Luke calls her, was Hellenist by birth; Lois was the first convert, instructed Eunice, and both brought up Timothy, so that he knew the faith well before Paul met him at Lystra. Draw the distinction plainly — a man may be well instructed in divine things, have an orthodox creed, and yet his heart not be changed; instruction precedes conversion and conversion should follow it. And do not pass over the praying: it is a rare thing that a man thanks God he is able to pray for others.

sides.position: The patriarchs and holy men of former times, Paul being of the same nation — so that his religion was not different from theirs but the same carried out and perfected, the Old Testament and the New being essentially one
Not Abraham and Isaac and the patriarchs, but the members of his own family, whose devotion he had inherited as a sacred family tradition
Simply that he and his ancestors alike served God, he being born a Jew and carefully educated in the knowledge of the true God
At the last parting from Paul
Not determinable — possibly the parting from the Ephesian elders, possibly the hour when he was first taught Christ crucified, possibly some interview otherwise unrecorded
Shed frequently, not only at the last parting

outliers.note: Alone stops to defend the weeping itself, on the ground that religion is not intended to make us stoics or savages, and alone draws from the passage that a very pure and warm friendship may hold between an old man and a young one, and that its warmth is not diminished by the near prospect of death.

Alone rewrites the whole sentence to show where the parenthesis begins and ends, alone dismisses Hofmann's theory that the tears were merely Timothy's grief on hearing of the arrest by letter, and alone raises and then refuses the conjecture that Lois, Eunice and Timothy were kinsfolk of Paul, Lystra lying no great distance from Tarsus — calling it an ingenious thought with no data to support it.

Alone remarks on the rarity of the thing Paul is doing, that it is very rare in the Christian church for a man to thank God particularly that he is enabled to pray for others, and alone praises the maintenance of a pure friendship across a long lapse of time and absence as deliverance from the fickleness that is the bane of friendships.

Alone presses the verb for dwelling — a word not applied to a transient guest but only to a settled inhabitant — and alone reads the mention of ancestors as consolation for a dying man, who is much refreshed by remembering the predecessors to whom he is going.

themes: I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day;
Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy;
When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also.

6.pericope_label: Stir up the gift of God: not the spirit of fear, but of power and love

schools.summary: The verb is not rouse in general but kindle: it is built on the word for a live coal and then for the bellows, so the sense is to fan into flame and keep blazing. Give the reason the charge was needed — Timothy was dispirited by the imprisonment and sinking at the prospect of holding Ephesus alone. On the laying on of hands, do not let the first letter and this one be played against each other: the presbytery were joined with the apostle in one act, and the possessive here is what any member of an ordaining body would naturally say to a younger man, a solemn personal appeal rather than a claim to sole authority. Deny firmly that any mysterious influence passed from the ordainers' hands imparting a holiness Timothy did not have before; the next verse names what was given. Render the first of the three gifts cowardice, and the last self-control rather than a sound mind.

Say why the reminder is given at all: because the apostle is persuaded of Timothy's faith and of the faith that stood in his family before him, he acts as a kind monitor and expects to succeed. Then name what the spirit of fear actually is in a minister — a pusillanimous temper afraid of what men will say or do, which sinks under the work of preaching, of opposing the errors of false teachers, and of reproving men for their sins. Such a spirit is not from God, and that fear brings a snare.

Press the metaphor to its conclusion, because it carries a doctrine: a fire not frequently stirred and fed goes out, so if Timothy had not continued a daily worker with God he would have received the grace of God in vain. The gift itself is the Holy Spirit and through him a particular power to preach and defend the truth. On the next verse, note the variant that reads bondage instead of cowardice, then set the whole against Sinai: the law was given with a terrible majesty that bred fear until even Moses trembled, while the gospel came in mildly, with nothing in it forbidding. Refuse the narrow rendering of the last word as mere self-possession — it means a clear understanding, a sound judgement, a rectified will, holy tempers, the whole soul harmonised. And give the arrangement: power and sobriety are two good extremes, love the tie between them, preventing fearfulness on the one hand and rashness on the other.

Stir it up as fire under the embers, and say plainly that the way to increase a gift is to use it, since to him that hath shall be given; neglected, it decays. Name the hindrance: the great obstacle to usefulness is slavish fear, and it was through base fear that the evil servant buried his talent and did not trade with it. Take the three gifts as a minister's own equipment — power, because they speak in the name of him who has all power in heaven and earth; love, because love to God and to the souls of men must inflame them in all their service; and a sound mind, meaning quietness of mind, since we are often discouraged by creatures of our own fancy which a solid thinking mind would answer at once.

debates.question: How do 'the laying on of my hands' here and 'the hands of the presbytery' in the first letter fit together?

sides.position: One act, in which the presbytery were joined with the apostle; the possessive is a personal appeal, not a claim of sole authority, and is exactly what any member of an ordaining body would say
Two distinct occasions: the presbytery ordained him, while Paul's hands earlier conferred the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, since none but apostles had power to give the Spirit
The question is left open; the possessive registers Paul's deep personal interest in Timothy
Self-control — the power that keeps passions, desires and impulses in wise subjection
Soberness of judgement: a mind well balanced, not feverish or excited, seeing things in their just proportions
Quietness of mind, a peaceable enjoyment of ourselves against the discouragements our own fancy manufactures
Far more than self-possession: a clear understanding, a sound judgement, a rectified will and holy tempers — the whole soul harmonised and regulated

outliers.note: Alone supplies the psychological occasion of the charge, that Timothy knew his master's career was ending and sank at the prospect of fighting alone at Ephesus, and alone passes on Wordsworth's suggestion that Paul had in mind the Roman law commanding that the eternal flame of the public hearth be watched, whose failure was an omen of disaster and whose watchers were severely punished.

Alone draws a conditional from the metaphor — that a fire unfed goes out, so that had Timothy not continued a daily worker with God he would have received the grace of God in vain — and alone reports the manuscript variant reading bondage in place of cowardice, and alone sets the verse against the giving of the law at Sinai.

Alone separates the two impositions of hands into distinct occasions on the ground that none but the apostles could give the Holy Ghost, and alone identifies the hindrance the verse addresses as slavish fear, the same fear that made the evil servant bury his talent.

Alone arranges the three gifts into a figure rather than a list: power and sobriety are two good extremes and love is the tie and temperament between them, preventing the two bad extremes of fearfulness and rashness.

themes: Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.

8.pericope_label: Be not ashamed: a holy calling, and death abolished by the appearing of Christ

schools.summary: Ask what power of God is meant, because the obvious answer is wrong: not the strength we receive from him to bear suffering, but the power he has already displayed towards us in our calling and salvation — so the argument runs from what has been done for us to what may be asked of us. Render the next clause suffer afflictions for the gospel rather than be a partaker of them. Press the negative in verse nine hard: works have nothing to do with inducing God to call us, and a purpose formed before the world began could not have rested on works foreseen. Then handle the great verse carefully. Abolished means rendered inoperative, not destroyed; the second noun is incorruption rather than immortality; and the article is worth showing — death carries it as a known and ruling power, while life and incorruption stand without it as things only lately revealed. Prove the novelty from the heathen: Cicero calls the hope of a future state a conjecture of ages, and Socrates at his death would not be positive which is the better state, the living or the dead.

Define the testimony before defending it: the gospel is so called because it comes from Christ and testifies of him — of his person and offices, his righteousness and sacrifice, his resurrection and session and intercession and second coming — and no preacher has cause to be ashamed of anything so true and so useful; whoever is ashamed of it, Christ will be ashamed of him another day. Then take the salvation that precedes the calling, which is easily missed: a special providence attends the elect from birth, preserving them through dangers and often from the grosser immoralities, and a chain of ordinary circumstances — the fixing of their habitations, their being brought to such a place and under such a ministry — leads on to the effectual calling.

Begin from the verse before: when fear is banished, evil shame flees away with it; and note that the cause of God's servants doing his work cannot be separated from the cause of God himself, so that to be ashamed of the prisoner is to be ashamed of the gospel. Read the closing phrase as a promise of proportion — a man never has more affliction than he has grace to bear, and a load carried by God's strength cannot be oppressive. On the last verse resist the easy claim that eternal life was unknown before: the Jews had it from their prophets and borrowed nothing from Christians, so what the gospel did was not to disclose the doctrine but to demonstrate it, since Christ lay under the empire of death, rose, and carried the same body up into heaven. Say of the abolishing that the sting is taken away and the thing itself turned into a blessing.

Locate the shame in method, not in nerve. Nothing is worse than measuring divine things by human reasonings; a man who tries it falls from the rock as surely as one who would look at the sun with human eyes is injured for trying, and that is how Marcion and Valentinus came to be ashamed of the divine economy — which was never a subject for shame but for glorying. Then turn the objects of shame over one by one. Death and chains are in themselves matters of reproach; but once the cause is added and the mystery seen rightly they are full of dignity, since that death saved a perishing world and joined earth to heaven, and those chains were the conversion of many. And do not stop at endurance: the text says not merely be unashamed of the sufferings but be partaker of them, so it is not enough not to blush at them — one must not blush to experience them.

debates.question: Whose power is meant by 'according to the power of God'?

sides.position: Not the power we receive from God for suffering, but the power God has displayed towards us in our calling and salvation
The strength supplied for the trial: no man has more affliction than he has grace to sustain, and a load borne by God's power cannot be oppressive

debates.question: Did the gospel first disclose life and immortality, or only demonstrate them?

sides.position: It disclosed them: the intimations among the wisest heathen were obscure and their hopes faint, and of the resurrection of the body they had no conception at all, so man would never have known these things without revelation

It demonstrated them: eternal life was not unknown to the Jews, who found it in their prophets and borrowed nothing from Christians, so what was new was the illustration in fact of what had existed in promise
Christ brought them to light chiefly by displaying them in his own resurrection body before eye-witnesses still living when Paul wrote

outliers.note: Alone assembles the classical testimony on the future state as evidence for the novelty of the doctrine, quoting Cicero calling the hope a conjecture of future ages, Seneca that it is what our wise men promise but do not prove, Pliny that neither soul nor body has more sense after death than before birth, and Socrates at his own death declining to be positive which is in the better state, the living or the dead.

Alone traces the possibility of shame to a method rather than a failure of nerve — the measuring of divine things by human reasonings — and alone refuses to let the charge stop at endurance, pointing out that the text says be partaker of the afflictions, so that it is not enough not to blush at them but one must not blush to experience them.

Alone observes the presence and absence of the article in the closing verse, that death carries it as a known and ruling power while life and incorruption stand without it as powers only lately revealed and known to few.

Alone finds a salvation antecedent to the calling: a providence attending the elect from birth and a chain of ordinary circumstances — the fixing of their habitations, their being brought under such a ministry — which leads on to the effectual calling.

themes: Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:

11.pericope_label: I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded he is able to keep

schools.summary: Correct the popular reading of the famous clause. The relative is a dative governed by the verb and the antecedent is simply unexpressed; this is not an indirect question, so the sense is not that Paul knows in whom he has believed but that he knows the person he has trusted. Then take the deposit as the soul, and give the evidence rather than asserting it: the imagery answers to the psalm, into thy hand I commend my spirit, whose Greek uses this very verb; Josephus, writing in the same age, calls the soul a deposit in a passage against suicide; and Philo, near a contemporary, uses the identical word. The verb for keeping means to guard against robbery or loss — a deposit as in a bank, the bank of heaven that no burglar can break. On the closing phrase, note that it needed no further description: the early Christians spoke of it so constantly that that day alone identified it.

Make the appointment twofold, from eternity in the counsel and purpose of God and in time by the church at Antioch at the express order of the Holy Ghost. Then let the titles carry their weight: if ever there was a preacher of the gospel Paul was one, who preached purely, powerfully, publicly, constantly, boldly and with all faithfulness. Say also what the sufferings were for — not for preaching only but for preaching to the Gentiles, which is what set both Jews and idolaters against him — and that he was appointed to the sufferings as truly as to the gospel.

Give the three titles their plain sense: the first is a herald, the second means sent immediately from God to man, and the third is one whose business is to instruct, the Gentiles particularly, in the doctrines of eternal life and the final incorruptibility of the body. On the deposit, do not settle what the text leaves open: it has been taken for his life, put into Christ's hands to be received again at the resurrection; for his soul, given to a faithful Creator whom wicked men cannot reach; and for the gospel itself, which God will preserve and cause to be proclaimed by others when Paul has sealed it with his blood. Rest the confidence where Paul rests it, on acquaintance with the goodness and mercy and power of Christ, and on knowing that one cannot confide in him in vain.

sides.position: Jesus Christ, whom Paul has trusted — and the construction is not an indirect question but a dative relative with its antecedent unexpressed
God the Father; and the tense should be given its force, whom I have trusted and still trust

debates.question: What is the deposit committed to him?

sides.position: The soul, on the evidence of the psalm Paul knew, of Josephus calling the soul a deposit, and of Philo using the identical word
The soul with all its immortal interests — there being no higher treasure a man can entrust to another, and the whole question of his happiness here and hereafter going with it

Undetermined: it may be his life, to be received again at the resurrection; his soul, beyond the reach of men who can only kill the body; or the gospel, which God will preserve and have proclaimed by others

outliers.note: Alone remarks on the strangeness of the three titles arriving at this point — a solitary prisoner awaiting death, deserted by his friends, rehearsing with solemn emphasis the dignities his Master gave him, because he means his last charge to carry the full authority of an apostle while admitting that these very sufferings came upon him through that office.

Alone builds the verse into a pastoral scheme and closes it with two images: a man shipwrecked who sees his child safe beside him on the shore will care little that a casket of jewels went overboard, and a man's great interests may be safer in a prison than in a palace, on a pallet of straw than on a bed of down.

Alone corrects the common rendering of the clause, insisting it is not an indirect question, and alone turns the noun into a picture, a deposit as in a bank, the bank of heaven which no burglar can break.

themes: Whereunto I am appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.

13.pericope_label: Hold fast the form of sound words; keep that good thing committed to thee

schools.summary: The noun means an outline or sketch, the plan of a building or a picture, and it is worth reporting what has been made of it — an exemplar fixed in the mind, adherence to the doctrine in its form as well as its substance, the profession of faith made at baptism. Then argue that what Paul gave Timothy was not a written creed, for two reasons: the text says he heard it, and had such a summary existed on paper it would have been reckoned inspired and would have found its way into the canon, since almost nothing would have been more carefully preserved. Draw the limited conclusion the argument will bear — a brief summary of doctrine is a legitimate convenience, but carries no binding authority over another man's conscience. On the next verse mark the reversal that is easy to miss: the deposit of the earlier verse was committed by Paul to God, this one is committed by God to Timothy, so God has made an investment in him which he must not let fail.

Take the verse as a rule for theological language and state it exactly. Words are not to be strived over for their own sake; but when a word has long served to convey a just idea of truth it is not to be lightly parted with, even though it is nowhere syllabically in Scripture, unless a better can be put in its room — and it is to be held most tenaciously when the evident design in dropping or changing it is to set aside the truth it signifies. Name the words at issue: trinity, unity, essence, person, imputed righteousness, satisfaction. Then say why the doctrines are called sound: not merely because they are sweet and pleasant but because they are salutary and nourishing, milk for babes and meat for strong men, over against teaching that is corrupt and eats as does a canker.

Argue the necessity of a fixed form from the other end: no man was left to invent a religion for his own use and after his own mind, since God alone knows what God can be pleased with, and without a revelation the inventions of men in religion would run to endless error. What is given is a plan and sketch of the original building, with the outlines of everything concerning man's welfare and God's glory. On faith and love keep the division clean: faith credits the divine doctrines and love reduces them all to practice, faith laying hold on Christ and obtaining the love by which every precept is cheerfully obeyed. And on the keeping, say plainly that without a continual spiritual energy man can do nothing.

Take the verse as evidence that Paul taught by word as well as by letter, since many things were delivered without writing — and therefore refuse the inference that anything in doctrine was imperfectly spoken. Use the image of the artist: Paul has impressed an image of virtue on his pupil, fixing in his soul a rule and model and outline of all that pleases God, so that Timothy need not go elsewhere for examples when everything has been deposited within him. Then explain why the command names the Spirit. A human soul entrusted with things so great is not sufficient of itself to keep them, for there are many robbers and thick darkness and an adversary who chooses his own hour; except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. The Spirit is our wall, our castle, our refuge. And raise the difficulty honestly — if the Spirit dwells in us and is itself our guard, what need of the commandment? That we may hold it fast and not banish it by our evil deeds.

debates.question: Was the 'form of sound words' a written document?

sides.position: No, and deliberately so: the text says Timothy heard it, and a written summary would have been reckoned inspired and preserved in the canon; the passage warrants a brief doctrinal summary as a convenience but gives it no binding authority over conscience
No, because Paul taught by word as well as letter and delivered many things without writing — which is precisely why nothing in doctrine should be supposed imperfectly spoken
The inspired formularies Timothy had heard from Paul's lips, such as the faithful sayings recurring in these letters

debates.question: What is the good thing committed to Timothy?

sides.position: The gospel entrusted to him to preach
The sound Christian doctrine he was to transmit to others
The treasure of the Catholic faith, to be kept unchanged and unalloyed

outliers.note: Alone reads the verse as a rule for theological vocabulary, arguing that a word long useful in conveying a just idea of truth is not to be parted with though it is nowhere syllabically in Scripture, and most of all when the evident aim in dropping it is to set aside the truth it carries — naming trinity, unity, essence, person, imputed righteousness and satisfaction.

Alone gives a reason for thinking the form was unwritten which turns on the canon itself: had such a summary existed on paper it would have been regarded as inspired and would have taken its place in Scripture, since almost none of the sacred writings would have been more sacredly preserved.

Alone notices that the deposit changes hands between the two verses — committed by Paul to God in the first, committed by God to Timothy in the second — and alone specifies how it is not to be kept: by no weak compliance with the scruples of false teachers, no timid accommodation, no yielding a little here and a little there.

Cites the verse for a purpose outside its context, as one of a chain of proofs that Paul and the apostles were full of the Holy Ghost, alongside the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, the earnest of the Spirit, and the quickening of mortal bodies by the Spirit that dwelleth in us.

themes: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.

15.pericope_label: All they in Asia be turned away; the house of Onesiphorus

schools.summary: Decide first where the desertion happened, because the alternatives are not equivalent: either Asiatic Christians in Rome deserted him at the trial, or churches in Asia itself repudiated their connection with him. Prefer the plainer sense, that it happened in Asia; then narrow the geography rather than the event, since Asia strictly taken would take in Mysia, Phrygia, Lydia and Caria, and a defection that wide is both improbable and unattested. Note that the words prove Timothy was in that region when the letter reached him, since otherwise he could not be supposed to know it, and that all must be general because a faithful exception is named two verses later. On Onesiphorus, weigh the evidence that he was recently dead — mercy is asked for his house rather than for him, and the phrase about that day — and take the refreshing to cover not only bodily needs but frequent visits and a disregard of what a man risked by open intimacy with a prisoner charged with treason.

Do not let the sweeping word stand unqualified: it cannot be said of every minister and every church and every member in Asia, so read it either of those who had followed Paul from Asia to Rome, or of a great number of the Asian churches and ministers. Then take the prayer for the household as a prayer in faith, resting on God's promises and on the instances in which he has shown mercy to the families of good men who served him faithfully and stood by his interest in times of trouble — as the house of Obed Edom was blessed for the sake of the ark it took care of.

Restrict the desertion to the Asiatics then at Rome, who found the apostle in disgrace and thought it dangerous to own him or his cause, and say plainly that no general defection of the Asian churches can be meant. Then let the fact land as an injury rather than a datum: what, from Paul the aged, the faithful soldier, and now the prisoner of Christ — a glorious trial, wisely reserved for the time when he stood on the borders of immortality. Reach for a modern parallel if one is at hand, as the picture of Francis Xavier inscribed apostle of the Indies, forsaken of all men, dying in a cottage. Then set the one faithful man against them all: he had acknowledged Paul and continued to do so, he and his household ministering to their imprisoned pastor and not ashamed of the cause for which he suffered, and as he showed mercy so mercy is asked for him.

Set the two men side by side and let the contrast preach itself. Note first that even in the best and purest ages of the church there were those who embraced the faith and afterwards revolted, and that Paul does not say they turned from the doctrine but that they turned from him, disowning him in the time of his distress — and we need not wonder, since many turned their backs on one far better than Paul. Then Onesiphorus, who refreshed him often and was not ashamed of his chain: a good man will seek opportunities of doing good and shun none that offer. On the prayer, resist the doctrinal use made of it — who told them Onesiphorus was dead, and can it be safe to ground a doctrine and practice of such importance on a mere supposition? Then take the phrase about that day as the awful thing it is, and draw the application: the best Christians will want mercy in that day, and if we would have it then we must seek it now.

debates.question: Where did the desertion take place?

sides.position: In Rome, among Asiatic Christians who were there at the time and would not own a prisoner in disgrace — no general defection of the Asian churches being meant
In Asia itself: large numbers of Christians, perhaps whole churches, repudiated their connection with the father of Gentile Christianity while he lay waiting for death
Not determinable — it is not known to what incident Paul refers

debates.question: Was Onesiphorus alive when Paul wrote?

sides.position: Recently dead: mercy is asked for his house rather than for him, and the prayer looks to that day; if he lost his life for visiting Paul it had probably just happened
Alive, since Paul would not have offered prayer for him if he were dead; and it cannot be safe to ground a doctrine and practice of such importance on a mere supposition

outliers.note: Alone lets the desertion register as an injury rather than a fact to be explained, exclaiming that it was from Paul the aged, the faithful soldier, now the prisoner of Christ, calling it a trial wisely reserved for the borders of immortality, and reaching for the picture of Francis Xavier inscribed apostle of the Indies, forsaken of all men, dying in a cottage.

Alone turns the two named deserters into a warning — that it is a sad thing when the only record of a man, the only evidence that he lived at all, is that he turned away from a friend — and alone reports the sceptical observation that the pretended lists of the seventy disciples seem to have been made by taking every name incidentally mentioned in the sacred books and not otherwise accounted for.

Alone rejects the Roman reading of the desertion although Chrysostom held it, alone limits Asia to the old Homeric sense of the country about the Cayster, and alone handles the praying-for-the-dead question with both sides in view, noting that Theodoret and Chrysostom held Onesiphorus living and wrote centuries before any controversy arose, and concluding that pressing this single disputed text in support of a controverted doctrine is extremely precarious.

themes: This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.
The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:

17.pericope_label: He sought me out very diligently: the Lord grant him mercy in that day

schools.summary: Let the searching tell you about the prison. That a man had to seek diligently before he found the apostle means a far more rigorous captivity than the one at the close of Acts, where Paul lived in his own hired house with a single guard; and whoever did the searching apparently did it at the risk of his life. On the doubled title in the next verse, decline the easy solution that the phrase had become a formulary and the repetition went unnoticed: keep both strictly, the first as Christ, which is what the title always means in Paul, the second as the Father, to whom judgment at the last day is elsewhere ascribed. Note that the verb for ministering has prompted the suggestion that Onesiphorus was a deacon at Ephesus, and that such an inference from one general expression is precarious. And note the comparative — Paul writes not that Timothy knows but that he knows better, these being things done at Ephesus where Timothy was and Paul was not.

Keep the occasion in view: Onesiphorus was at Rome on business of his own when he sought out a prisoner, and the mercy asked in return is not something the apostle can repay himself. He knew it was out of his power, so he uses the interest he has at the throne of grace on the man's behalf. By mercy understand the mercy of Christ unto eternal life, the crown of righteousness and everlasting happiness, which is a free grant through him and the effect of pure grace, not of merit — which is worth saying plainly in a verse where one man's kindness is being answered by another man's prayer.

Say why the searching was hard: Paul was confined closely and privately, so that a friend from Asia with business in Rome had to hunt for him, having already entertained him at Ephesus and now seeking him in prison. Two sayings will carry the point — pure love feels no loads, and here was a friend that sticketh closer than a brother. On the doubled title, report the construction that makes the first the Father and the second Christ the Judge, but treat the doubling as probably a Hebraism, on the pattern of similar forms in Genesis and Exodus, and read the whole simply as a prayer that the man be saved now by grace and receive mercy then unto eternal life. Then stand back and let the chapter land: a life of perils and superabundant labours, leaving a track of light wherever it went, ending in old age neglected, in prison and in chains, and still unshaken — feeling no evil and fearing none, because sin had lost its power and death its sting. That is the happiness of which heathenism could speak but which it could not reach, not knowing the source it must come from.

debates.question: How should the doubled 'the Lord' in the prayer be construed?

sides.position: Strictly, and as two persons: the first is Christ, as the title always is in Paul, and the second the Father, to whom judgment at the last day is ascribed
Probably a Hebraism on the pattern of similar forms in Genesis and Exodus — a prayer that he be saved now by grace and find mercy then unto eternal life
An echo rather than a construction: Onesiphorus sought and found Paul, and the prayer is that he may find mercy from the Lord as he found the apostle

outliers.note: Closes the chapter with a peroration on Paul himself rather than on the text — the perils and superabundant labours, the track of light left wherever he went, the old age neglected and in chains and still unshaken — and quotes a poet's lines on the man who could know the causes of things and put fear and inexorable fate and the roar of greedy Acheron beneath his feet, observing that this was the happiness heathenism could name but not attain, not knowing the source it must proceed from.

Alone turns the searching into a question for the reader, that not everyone even among professors of religion would take the trouble in a great and splendid city to seek out a Christian brother, or even a minister, who was a prisoner — and expects this man to be among those told at the last that they came to Christ in prison.

Alone remarks how the passage steps over the interval between death and judgment, Paul's thought passing straight to the day when the great white throne is set up; and suggests that the expectation of a speedy coming, which he certainly shared, almost effaced the waiting time from the minds of the early Christians.

Alone notices that Paul writes not that Timothy knows but that he knows better than the writer does, the only example of that comparative in the New Testament, since the kindnesses in question were done at Ephesus where Timothy was and Paul was not.

themes: But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me.
The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.
